views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the table through the remainder of the 90-day window and keep high-level talks with Lighthizer/Mnuchin open. Signal willingness to specify large, verifiable purchases of U.S. agriculture, energy, and manufactures to shrink the bilateral imbalance, but do not lock in those purchases—or any structural rewrite of industrial policy—until Washington puts a matching tariff freeze or rollback on the table. Do not add new tariff or hostage-style retaliation during this window; further escalation now would make the March 1 List-3 hike to 25% more likely, not less.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% since 24 Sep 2018), and the G20 pause only delayed—did not cancel—the scheduled List-3 jump to 25% if there is no agreement by early March. That is a direct hit on the export machine: U.S. customs imports from China fell from $49.9B in Sep 2018 to $41.3B in Jan 2019 (−17%), and contemporaneous reporting shows 2018 GDP at 6.6% (slowest since 1990), Q4 at 6.4%, December exports/imports contracting, and Guangdong factories shutting early as orders dry up. Firm-level targeting has also jumped: ZTE was cut off in Apr 2018, and on 28 Jan 2019 DOJ unsealed fraud/sanctions charges against Huawei and Meng and formally requested extradition—the same week Liu He is in talks—while Beijing already detained Kovrig and Spavor. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors, Huawei, export-hub unemployment risk), but not +1.0: talks are live, the 10%→25% hike is still suspended, and Beijing has policy space (five RRR cuts, pledged tax/infra support, no hard-landing print). Action should stay near zero rather than escalate because a new Chinese tariff or detention wave would give U.S. hawks a pretext to let the March cliff hit and possibly extend tariffs to the remaining ~$267B; the May 2018 purchase-only “trade war on hold” collapsed within days when the White House proceeded with the $50B action. Mid-January talks already showed the split: purchases are discussable, structural IP/tech-transfer/enforcement is not closed, and Ross publicly said the sides are “miles and miles” apart. Concede_purchases is premature—no matching U.S. offer exists. Full rollback or further retaliation would either surrender leverage or blow up the only pause we have. Negotiate: explore de-escalation, keep purchases as bargaining chips, hold the line on “unacceptable” structural items, and use the remaining weeks to test whether Trump’s deal hunger outweighs Lighthizer’s enforcement demands.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports already under Section 301; List 3 still scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% if the 90-day window fails around 1 Mar 2019
Huawei/Meng criminal charges and extradition request unsealed 28 Jan 2019, coinciding with high-level talks; prior ZTE denial order and Canadian detentions keep a second, non-tariff front open
Real-economy stress: official 2018 GDP 6.6% (28-year low), Dec trade contraction, IMPCH −17% Sep–Jan, Guangdong export-hub order loss and job-risk reports
Talks are live but asymmetric: China can move on purchases; U.S. still demands structural IP/tech-transfer changes plus verification, and the May 2018 purchase truce collapsed

Escalating now raises the odds of the March tariff cliff and a possible further U.S. list; pre-conceding purchases or industrial-policy rewrite without a U.S. tariff concession repeats a failed 2018 sequence

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.

G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou...
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
U.S. Imports of Goods from China fell from 49938 (2018-09) to 41303 (2019-01); change_pct about -17.3%.
China's economy cooled in Q4 under faltering domestic demand and bruising U.S. tariffs; 2018 growth 6.6%, slowest since 1990; Q4 6.4%; Dec exports/imports shrank; Guangdong factories shut early.
Little progress on structural issues in January Beijing talks; China offered to raise purchases to cut the deficit; Ross said the countries are miles and miles from resolving differences.
USTR emphasized structural changes and verification/enforcement; progress on purchases but little on structural reform; May 2018 purchase deal was overruled within days.
Huawei/Meng indictment unveiled as Liu He arrived for talks; Beijing accused the U.S. of using state power to stifle Huawei and urged revocation of the arrest warrant.
